extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of natural philosophy / early‑modern natural philosophers and educated lay readership
extracted.subtask_description: A didactic account (natural‑philosophical/experimental) of what produces winds, how they behave (trade winds/monsoons), and experiments that demonstrate mechanisms (compression, rarefaction, heating, cooling, fermentation, motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Winds as necessary and purposeful for sustaining life
rubrics_metrics.description: The constancy and effects of winds (transporting vapours, producing rain, replenishing rivers, enabling mills and navigation) prevent the destruction of most living creatures and therefore argue against the idea that winds are mere accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument from necessity: if winds were accidental, moist vapours would fall back at their sources, dry lands and rivers would fail, and many creatures would perish. The practical benefits to mankind (mills, ships, transport of goods, draining land) reinforce the appearance of providential design. Examples and rhetorical comparisons (watering-pot, aqueducts) are used to show that small instruments having purpose implies greater instruments (winds) also imply design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy/regularity of certain winds as evidence of order
rubrics_metrics.description: Many winds (notably Trade Winds and Monsoons) show fixed, determinate behaviour — e.g., Trade/Passage winds blow from the same quarter year‑round; Monsoons reverse seasonally — behaviour comparable to clockwork, not random chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observations (sea‑faring and geographic reports, Halley, charts) to demonstrate that some winds blow in a consistent course (e.g., the Trade‑Winds blow from roughly the same quarter up to about 30° latitude; Monsoons blow half the year from one quarter and the other half from the opposite). Emphasize consequences: without such regularity voyages and commerce would be impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade‑Winds and Monsoons: empirical regularities to record
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific observed regularities: (I) between the Tropicks there always reigns an easterly trade in certain zones; (II) Trade‑Winds extend roughly to 30° latitude; (III) certain coasts (e.g., Guinea) have persistent south‑west winds; (IV) the South‑Sea has easterly trade; (V) northern Indian Sea exhibits monsoon reversals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the geographic extents and seasonal behavior (Halley's and others' observations). These are given as particulars to be consulted in works of Halley, Verulam, Varenus, Mariotte and sea‑charts/atlases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment I — Contraction of the containing space (bellows effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: If air is shut up and the place containing it is rendered narrower (space contracted), the air is pressed and forces its way through passages, thereby producing a blast or wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations: blowing with the mouth, using bellows, or devices where water ascends in a cistern contracting an air space and expelling air through a narrow tube (Hero's hollow vessel). Examples include organ pipes, blowing fires, and smelting when air is forced through narrow passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment II — Wind as watery vapours (alipile hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some philosophers propose that wind consists not chiefly of motion of air but of watery vapours; experiments (heated hollow brass globe with orifice — alipile/wind‑globe) show vapours rushing out like a violent wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an alternative hypothesis: the experiment of heating then cooling a globe producing violent outflow supports the idea that vapours can generate air‑streams. The author records the hypothesis but does not fully adjudicate its probability here; reference to figs and prior discussion is given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment III — Motion of solids through air generates wind
rubrics_metrics.description: A body moving swiftly through air causes the surrounding air to follow and produce a wind behind it; demonstrated by striking the air with the hand or by cannon‑balls and falling hailstones producing gusts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple tests: strike the air with a closed hand, drop small bullets into water to observe rising air bubbles created by the moving bodies, and observe the blast felt from cannon balls. Use of high‑speed bodies (hail, cannon balls) illustrates violent local winds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment IV — Fermentation/effervescence produces air currents
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing effervescent matters (liquid with solids or two liquids) produces fermentation that exhales air/vapours violently from the vessel — a form of wind generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: dropping iron filings into spirit of saltpetre, mixing acid and alkaline spirits (spirit of salt‑ammoniac with potash, hartshorn spirit), or other combinations that effervesce and expel air. Care: do not seal vessels too long as strong fermentation can burst glass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment V — Combustion of sulphureous mixtures generates violent outflows
rubrics_metrics.description: Inflaming mixtures of saltpetre with sulphur, antimony, or salt of tartar can produce very violent protrusion of air and smoke that behave like strong winds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical demonstration: mix antimony with saltpetre (or sulphur with saltpetre), enclose and apply fire; observe quick streams of smoke/air forcing through tubes. Use as analogy for hurricanes or local violent winds; note associated phenomena (temporary duration, localness, concurrent earthquakes, dead fish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment VI — Increase of the elastic power of air produces winds (expansion‑driven outflow)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the particles of air are pressed together (increasing elasticity), they expand or rush out with great swiftness producing a wind (as in a wind‑gun or compressed air in a narrow neck).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations: compressed air driving a bullet from a wind‑gun; blowing strongly into a small bottle with narrow mouth and releasing to observe rapid outflow. Suggests that sudden local increases of elasticity may explain gusts or blasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment VII — Diminution/weakening (vacuum) causes inrush wind
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing or diminishing the quantity or strength of air in a place (creating a vacuum or weakening elastic faculty) causes the surrounding stronger air to rush in violently — producing a wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations: use an air‑pump or simple bottle/bladder suction experiments (extracting internal air, then inverting and releasing to let external air rush in). References to Guericke and Papin machines and to numerical estimates (velocity calculations) are cited to show potential violence of such inrushes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment VIII — Cold produces winds by weakening elastic faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: When one air is colder than an adjacent air (and otherwise similar), the colder air's elastic faculty is weakened so that the less cold (stronger) air expands into it and produces a wind against the colder air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thermometer operation and simple bottle + bladder + snow/salt experiment: cool the air enclosed in a bottle with snow and salt to weaken its elasticity, then prick the bladder to watch external air rush in as a wind. Historical frost observations cited (12 January 1709).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment IX — Warmth produces winds by expanding air
rubrics_metrics.description: Warmth dilates and rarifies air, causing it to move toward places of less resistance and produce currents/outflows (winds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations: heat the globular part of an inverted bottle (mouth over a plate with water) with a glowing coal to see rarified air escaping in bubbles; stronger heat (hot water around a bladder‑covered bottle) produces a stronger blast. Connects to solar heating as mechanism for some trade winds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment X — Suspension/cessation of warmth causes returning winds
rubrics_metrics.description: When warmth that previously dilated and expelled air ceases, the included air cools and its expansive power weakens; external air then passes in with a returning wind to fill the rarified space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bottle + warming + bladder experiment: heat a bottle until air rushes out, tie a warm wet bladder over the mouth and invert; when internal air cools, make a pin‑hole in the bladder and observe the immediate inrush of external air through the water as a wind. Relate to diurnal or seasonal cooling effects on wind patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment XI — Upward motion (ascending columns) produces air currents
rubrics_metrics.description: When air is rarified (by heat) beneath a vertical column (e.g., under the sun) it will ascend, producing an upward current and associated circulations (straight ascending columns of air).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Halley: vertical ascent under solar heating leads to columns and consequent atmospheric motions. Use as part of an explanation of larger scale circulations and convection contributing to wind patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple converging experimental lines to infer causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than claiming a single simple cause, the text advances multiple experiments and observations (contraction, rarefaction, combustion, motion, vacuum, heating/cooling, fermentation) as complementary mechanisms that demonstrate how winds may arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine practical demonstrations (bellows, bottles, heated globes, fermentation, compressed air experiments) with geographic and seafaring observations (Halley, Mariotte, Verulam) to form a reasoned picture of wind generation. The author advises humility but encourages consulting the cited experimental literature for fuller proof.
